title: Cricothyroid Subluxation (Adjunct to Medialization)
source_label: Operative Techniques in Laryngology (2024), Ch 49 Cricothyroid Subluxation
indications: An adjunct to medialization laryngoplasty (with or without arytenoid repositioning) for unilateral vocal fold paralysis when the paralyzed fold is short and flaccid, with poor pitch range and a weak or asymmetric mucosal wave. It may be planned from preoperative assessment or chosen intraoperatively when glottic closure is good but pitch and vibration remain poor. Subluxing the cricothyroid joint on the paralyzed side draws the inferior thyroid cornu anteriorly over the cricoid, recreating the cricothyroid muscle vector. This rotates the anterior commissure attachment away from the cricoarytenoid joint, lengthening and tensing the fold. Do not perform when the thyroid ala is fractured or at risk of fracture from the medialization window.
setup: Awake sedation with local anesthesia so pitch and voice can be tested during tensioning
Transnasal flexible laryngoscope on a monitor to judge fold length and closure
Standard thyroplasty exposure already completed on the paralyzed side
2-0 polypropylene on a narrow semicircle needle, right-angle (vascular) clamp, fine scissors or Cottle elevator, a cutting needle for direct cartilage anchoring, and a plating set for alar fracture
Separate the joint during the exposure, then complete medialization and any arytenoid procedure, and place and tension the subluxation suture last
landmarks: Inferior cornu of the thyroid cartilage
Cricothyroid muscle anterior and inferior to the cornu
Recurrent laryngeal nerve immediately posterior to the cricothyroid joint
Thyroplasty window and lower alar margin
danger: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury behind the joint
Fracture of the thyroid ala, especially near the window
Cricoid fracture or airway entry when passing the suture
Suture slippage with loss of tension
steps: Decide to add the subluxation

After medialization, assess the glottis and voice. If closure is good but the fold looks short with poor pitch range and a weak mucosal wave, proceed; confirm the thyroid ala is intact, because an existing or likely alar fracture is a contraindication.
Sequence the procedures

Skeletonize the cornu and separate the cricothyroid joint during the initial exposure, then complete the medialization implant and any arytenoid adduction or arytenopexy so final glottic position is set. Place and tension the subluxation suture last, since it changes fold length and is tuned against the finished medialization.
Skeletonize the inferior cornu

Remove the cricothyroid muscle immediately anterior and inferior to the inferior cornu, release the inferior constrictor from its posterior surface, and clear soft tissue over the midline cricoid. Bipolar helps hemostasis. Stay right on cartilage, because the recurrent laryngeal nerve passes just posterior to the cricothyroid joint.
Separate the joint

Place scissor blades against the posterolateral cricoid with the tips straddling the cricothyroid joint and divide it, or use a Cottle elevator. Scissors are less likely to fracture the cornu. Incomplete release limits anterior movement of the cornu, while dissection beyond the joint risks the nerve.
Anchor the cornu

Pass 2-0 polypropylene around the neck of the freed inferior cornu with a narrow semicircle needle or right-angle clamp, positioned as high on the neck as possible, and tie it leaving equal limbs. If the cornu is short, broad, or fractured, pass a cutting needle through the cornu or inferior thyroid cartilage edge instead.
Pass under the cricoid

Pass the needled limb submucosally beneath the anterior cricoid ring at the midline. Follow the needle curve gently so the cricoid does not fracture and the needle stays outside the airway lumen. Leave the free limb from the cornu knot ready for tying.
Tension the suture

Bring the free cornu limb to the cricoid limb and sequentially increase and decrease tension while the patient sustains a vowel. A correct vector produces pitch that rises with tension and falls as it is released, with visible fold lengthening. If no pitch change occurs, reposition the suture.
Set the tension

Choose the final tension by perceptual voice quality and endoscopic fold length and symmetry. Only moderate tension is usually needed; excessive pull can over-tense the fold, raise pitch unnaturally, or cut through cartilage.
Secure the knot

Use an initial slip knot to hold the chosen tension, then add several throws, because polypropylene is prone to slip. Recheck the voice after the knot is set and confirm on endoscopy that closure from the medialization has not been disturbed by the change in laryngeal geometry.
Manage fractures

If the inferior cornu fractures, place a suture through thyroid cartilage near the fracture line and use it in the same way to complete the subluxation. If the thyroid ala fractures, reduce and fix it and reconsider tensioning, since alar fracture is a contraindication to the subluxation.
Close

Obtain hemostasis, reapproximate the strap muscles, and close in layers as for medialization laryngoplasty, with a drain only if dissection was extensive. Check the airway endoscopically before the patient leaves the room.
exit_check: Fold lengthened with improved pitch and voice quality on sustained vowel
Knot secure with multiple throws and no cartilage fracture
postop: Observation for airway edema or hematoma per thyroplasty routine
Short voice rest, then voice therapy
Stroboscopy at follow-up for pitch range, fold length, and mucosal wave

early: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury from joint dissection
Cricoid or alar fracture recognized intraoperatively
late: Suture slippage or pull-through with loss of pitch benefit
Over-tensioned fold with high or strained voice

attending_followup: What problem does cricothyroid subluxation address that medialization does not?
The short, flaccid paralyzed fold with poor pitch range and weak mucosal wave; medialization closes the gap but does not restore length or tension.
Mechanically, what does the subluxation do?

It draws the inferior thyroid cornu anteriorly relative to the cricoid on the paralyzed side, recreating the cricothyroid muscle vector. The anterior commissure attachment moves away from the cricoarytenoid joint, lengthening and tensing the fold.
When the thyroid ala is fractured or at risk of fracture from the medialization window.
Where is the recurrent laryngeal nerve relative to the cricothyroid joint and how is it protected?
Immediately posterior to the joint. Stay on cartilage when removing cricothyroid and inferior constrictor fibers and dividing the joint, and favor bipolar for hemostasis.
How do you confirm the correct suture vector intraoperatively?
Pitch should rise as tension increases and fall as it is released during sustained phonation, with endoscopic fold lengthening.
